# Quasiconcave projective shadows do not retain the sharp continuous constant

This closes a proposed auxiliary route, not OC. Projecting positive fibers
along rays from an actual mixed-integer point produces nested convex sets,
but quasiconcavity of the resulting density alone is insufficient.

## 1. The elementary projective-shadow formula

Let (g,x0) belong to a convex mixed-integer body, and fix a primitive integer
base direction v. For positive integers k with nonempty fibers put

    T_k=(K_(g+kv)-x0)/k.

Convexity and x0 in K_g imply T_l contains T_k whenever 0<l<k. Indeed
(l/k)K_(g+kv)+(1-l/k)x0 is contained in K_(g+lv). Under the change of
variables x=x0+k t, the positive-ray fiber measure becomes the density

    f(t)=sum_(k>0) k^d 1_(T_k)(t).

Thus its superlevel sets are nested convex sets. In general f is only
quasiconcave; no log-concavity has been established. A cap through (g,x0)
restricts along the ray to an affine halfspace in t, because its margin is
k times a fixed affine function of t.

## 2. Exact counterexample to a quasiconcave continuous depth bound

Let T={(x,y):x>=0,y>=0,x+y<=1}, and T_small=(1/10)T. Consider the probability
measure

    mu=(9/10) Uniform(T)+(1/10) Uniform(T_small).

Its density has two positive levels, with superlevel sets T and T_small.
It is therefore quasiconcave. Write the barycentric coordinates
lambda0=1-x-y, lambda1=x, lambda2=y. The three closed halfspaces

    H0={lambda0>=2/5},
    H1={lambda1>=3/10},
    H2={lambda2>=3/10}

cover the whole plane: their thresholds sum to1, as do the three
barycentric coordinates. Every point consequently belongs to at least one
of these caps. The small triangle lies wholly in H0 and misses H1,H2.
A vertex cap {lambda_i>=a} occupies fraction (1-a)^2 of T. Hence

    mu(H0)=1/10+(9/10)(3/5)^2=53/125=424/1000,
    mu(H1)=mu(H2)=(9/10)(7/10)^2=441/1000.

It follows for EVERY center y in the plane that

    depth_mu(y)<=441/1000 < 4/9,

with exact gap 4/9-441/1000=31/9000. This is a finite closed-cap certificate,
not a numerical optimization. It also explains why the ordinary log-concave
radialization theorem cannot be applied merely from nested shadow levels.

## 3. Exact integer-power weights and an actual mixed convex realization

The density proportional to 1_T+4 1_D, where D=(1/100,1/100)+(1/10)T,
has normalized inner mixture weight1/26. Use the three thresholds

    a0=177/500, a1=a2=323/1000.

They sum to1. The small translated triangle D lies wholly in cap0 and
misses caps1,2, so

    p0=1/26+(25/26)(323/500)^2=114329/260000,
    p1=p2=(25/26)(677/1000)^2=458329/1040000.

The latter is larger, and

    4/9 - 458329/1040000 = 35039/9360000 >0.

These integer-power weights arise from positive fibers of an actual convex
body, with the ray center in the interior of its own positive-area fiber.
Put x0=(1/50,1/50), let K0=x0+[-1/1000,1/1000]^2, and set

    K1=T, K2=2D-x0,
    C=conv(({0} times K0) union ({1} times K1) union ({2} times K2)).

The endpoint fibers are exactly K0,K2. Its index1 fiber is exactly K1,
because

    (K0+K2)/2=D+[-1/2000,1/2000]^2 subset int(T).

There are no other integer indices in its projection [0,2]. All three
fibers have positive area, C is a full-dimensional convex body, and
(0,x0) lies in the relative interior of the index0 fiber. The positive-ray
shadow sets are T1=T-x0 and T2=D-x0, giving precisely the density above
up to translation. The three translated closed caps provide the same
strictly sub-gamma2 continuous depth upper bound.

This defeats the proposed implication from convex mixed fibers and nested
projective shadows to the sharp ordinary continuous center bound. It is
not a claim about the depth of the original mixed-integer set, whose
halfspaces and candidate centers are different.
